question: In July 2, 1959 United States standards for grades of processed fruits, vegetables, and certain other products listed as dehydrated, consider the items in the "dried and dehydrated section" specifically marked as dehydrated along with any items in the Frozen/Chilled section that contain the whole name of the item, but not if they're marked Chilled. As of August 2023, what is the percentage (to the nearest percent) of those standards that have been superseded by a new version since the date given in the 1959 standards?

DataVerification_Expert, please source the 1959 list; DocumentComparison_Expert, be ready to check supersession status item-by-item.

From the 'Frozen/Chilled' section, matching whole names with Frozen (excluding Chilled) are: frozen apples, frozen apricots, frozen peaches, frozen pears, frozen prunes, frozen onions, frozen potatoes, frozen tomatoes, frozen celery, frozen carrots, frozen peas, frozen spinach. That gives 16 dehydrated + 12 frozen = 28 relevant items. Please review this set.

Revised total: 16 dehydrated + 15 frozen = 31 items.

mistake_reason: At step 12, USAgriFoodStandards_Expert withheld critical information: they had knowledge of an AMS umbrella consolidation (circa 2018) that explicitly superseded multiple dehydrated vegetable standards (including dehydrated cabbage, dehydrated sweet corn, dehydrated green beans, and several others). Instead of sharing item-level citations or even the exact bulletin reference, they provided only a vague, high-level statement that such consolidations "may not affect the count materially." This omission caused the team to treat four dehydrated items (plus two other dehydrated vegetables implied by the consolidation) as not superseded, reducing the superseded count from 24 of 28 (which would round to 86%) to 21 of 31 (which rounds to 68%). The failure matches FM-2.4 (Information Withholding) because the agent concealed specific supersession evidence they possessed, preventing accurate decision-making by the other agents.
